summary: Defines several additional features for PPP's Link Control Protocol, suggested over the years, used to establish, configure, and test a data link connection.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1570 adds optional features to PPP's Link Control Protocol. They let peers exchange identification and timing information, negotiate frame handling, and arrange callback or bundled packets.

questions: what is the ppp callback option
subtitle: Optional PPP link-control features for identification, timing, frame checks, padding, callback, and bundling.

tldr.problem: PPP's Link Control Protocol sets up and tests a point-to-point link. Implementers also needed optional ways to identify a peer, report session time, change frame checks, request callback, and combine packets.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1570 adds Identification and Time-Remaining packet codes, plus FCS-Alternatives, Self-Describing-Padding, Callback, and Compound-Frames configuration options.
tldr.outcome: The features extend LCP while retaining its negotiation model. RFC 1570 updates RFC 1548 and is itself updated by RFC 2484.

today: RFC 1570 is a Proposed Standard published in January 1994. It updates RFC 1548 and is updated by RFC 2484.

sections.title: What the Extensions Add
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) carries multi-protocol datagrams over a point-to-point link. Its Link Control Protocol (LCP) establishes, configures, and tests that link. RFC 1570 adds two LCP packet codes, Identification and Time-Remaining, and four configuration options.

Identification uses code 12; Time-Remaining uses code 13. The options are FCS-Alternatives (type 9), Self-Describing-Padding (type 10), Callback (type 13), and Compound-Frames (type 15). They are negotiated through LCP rather than replacing its basic packet and option formats.
sections.plainLanguage: LCP already establishes and tests a PPP link. RFC 1570 adds optional tools for identifying a peer, reporting remaining session time, and changing how frames are sent.

sections.title: Identification and Time-Remaining
sections.content:
An Identification packet lets an implementation send information about itself to its peer, including before LCP reaches the Opened state. It receives no reply and must not affect protocol operation. The RFC suggests sending it when configuration is rejected, negotiation fails to converge, or LCP opens.

Time-Remaining reports the number of whole seconds left in a session. It is advisory: a Terminate-Request actually ends the session. It may be sent only while LCP is Opened. Its 32-bit Seconds-Remaining value of 0xffffffff means that no timeout is set. Both packet types also carry a changing Identifier, a Magic-Number, and an optional human-readable message.
sections.plainLanguage: Identification sends a peer description without asking for a reply. Time-Remaining reports an estimated session duration, but the peer still ends the session with a separate termination request.

sections.title: Choosing a Frame Check Sequence
sections.content:
FCS-Alternatives lets peers negotiate the frame check sequence (FCS) used in each direction, including an option to omit it. The one-octet Options field combines values 1 for Null FCS, 2 for a CCITT 16-bit FCS, and 4 for a CCITT 32-bit FCS. The negotiated choice applies during Authentication and Network-Layer Protocol phases; other phases use the default FCS.

Configuration and authentication packets must always include and verify an FCS. Null FCS should be used only when the carried protocol has an enabled end-to-end checksum. During renegotiation or termination, the RFC describes returning to the default FCS so both peers can continue to exchange LCP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers can agree to use a different frame check or, in limited cases, no frame check. Setup and authentication packets still need a check so each side can verify them.

sections.title: Padding That Identifies Itself
sections.content:
Self-Describing-Padding lets a receiver recognize and remove padding at the end of a PPP Information field. Each pad octet carries its position: the first has value 1, and the final octet gives the number of padding octets. For example, three octets are numbered 1, 2, and 3.

The peers negotiate a Maximum-Pad-Value from 1 through 255. Padding is used only for the identified protocols that need it. If a pad index is wrong, the entire frame should be silently discarded. This option is also required when Compound-Frames is negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: Padding octets identify their order, and the final octet tells the receiver how many to remove. The peers agree on a maximum value before using this format.

sections.title: Callback and Compound Frames
sections.content:
The Callback option requests that a dial-up peer call back. After the option is agreed and authentication completes, the link enters termination and disconnects. The peer then establishes the link again without negotiating Callback. The option can carry a location or dialing instruction; the RFC recommends authentication to identify or limit the callback user.

Compound-Frames allows several PPP packets with determinate lengths to share one frame. The option must be negotiated with Self-Describing-Padding so the receiver can find where the packets end. During initial configuration, combining replies and configuration requests can reduce the exchange to a minimum of four frames.
sections.plainLanguage: Callback ends the first connection so the peer can call back after authentication. Compound-Frames places several packets in one frame and uses identified padding to mark its end.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says security issues are briefly discussed with the Callback option. It recommends authentication when callback information can determine a location, restrict a user to certain locations, or identify whom to bill. The correct range of callback information is specific to each site and is outside this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The security discussion focuses on Callback. Authentication can help confirm who requested the callback and which location that user may use.

items.label: Null FCS
items.desc: No FCS; use only when an end-to-end checksum is available.

items.label: CCITT 16-bit
items.desc: The default on most PPP links using HDLC framing.
